title: What Hogwarts Gets Right About Schooling
author: Aldeman, Chad
summary: Chad Aldeman uses Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry as a vehicle for arguing that cognitive science supports a curriculum model built on foundational knowledge, reading, essay writing, memorization, and high expectations — the elements that modern edtech and progressive pedagogy have systematically devalued. At Hogwarts, students read voluminously, write essays by hand, memorize spells, pass rigorous exams, and build deep factual knowledge before applying it creatively. Aldeman argues this is precisely what the cognitive science literature recommends: background knowledge enables comprehension, and creative application depends on prior mastery of fundamentals. The article challenges the false dichotomy between knowledge and creativity, showing that Rowling's fictional school accidentally models what a knowledge-rich curriculum looks like in practice. He concludes that the renewed interest in knowledge-rich curricula is not nostalgia but a return to what cognitive science has always shown about how human learning works.
points: Hogwarts students read voluminously, write essays by hand, memorize spells and potions, and pass rigorous exams — which is precisely what cognitive science recommends for deep learning.
The dichotomy between knowledge and creativity is false: creative application depends on prior mastery of the foundational knowledge that makes it possible.
Modern edtech systematically devalues the knowledge-building activities — sustained reading, writing, memorization — that cognitive science shows are essential to genuine understanding.
Rowling accidentally modeled a knowledge-rich curriculum because knowledge-rich curriculum is what serious schooling has always looked like before it was disrupted by progressive ideology.
The renewed interest in knowledge-rich curricula is not nostalgia — it is a return to what decades of cognitive science research have consistently demonstrated about how humans learn.
quotes: These essays are not personal reflections like, “How did this spell make you feel?” or “Describe a time you showed courage.” Instead, these are research papers, and they’re often about historical figures and events that require multiple sources.

Rowling imagined a school where reading books is worthwhile, that writing helps students think, that knowledge should accumulate over time, and that rigorous assessments can open doors rather than close them.
And yet, decades of cognitive science suggests that Hogwarts’ old school approach may have done a better job teaching its students to think than technological shortcuts would today.
Students cannot analyze history without knowing facts and people and dates, and they can’t solve complex math problems without being fluent in basic foundational skills.
Students read books, write essays, memorize key facts, learn from expert teachers, and demonstrate what they’ve learned through demanding, standardized exams.
Because these assessments carry such high stakes, the wizarding world makes a tremendous effort to ensure they are rigorous, consistent, and credible.
Their classes revolve around substantial textbooks like The Standard Book of Spells, A History of Magic, and The Monster Book of Monsters.
